hero.name: Yanrui Chen
hero.role: MSc in Artificial Intelligence · Real-time algorithms for wearable robotics
hero.summary: I am an MSc in Artificial Intelligence candidate at CUHK. At Shenzhen Yunmostar I build EMG-and-IMU gait control and IMU-based pose algorithms for a consumer exoskeleton: scene-transition recognition, then the input pipeline, six-IMU calibration and error attribution behind sparse-IMU human pose estimation. Here a model only matters if it meets its latency budget and its numbers survive an audit. Before this I studied electronic information and computer engineering at CUHK-Shenzhen, and built projects in medical image segmentation, LLM fine-tuning and a high-concurrency auction backend.
facts: BEng Electronic Information and Computer Engineering
highlights: Defined the scene-transition recognition task for a consumer exoskeleton and delivered a frozen ONNX + TensorRT model behind a ROS 2 topic interface on a Jetson Orin Nano
Built the sparse-IMU input pipeline (6-DoF ESKF + walking calibration) and ran the six-IMU offline calibration and Allan-variance analysis behind a three-layer pose error study
Fine-tuned a 90M-parameter ViT encoder to lift prompt-free ultrasound lesion IoU from 0.093 to 0.737
Held 98.4% bid success and 65 ms P99 round-trip at 1,000 concurrent WebSocket connections per live room (local benchmark)

paragraphs: I build systems where a model has to survive contact with the physical world. At Yunmostar I defined the scene-transition recognition task for a consumer exoskeleton: telling whether the wearer is starting to climb stairs, descend them, go up or down a slope, or return to level ground, so assist torque can change smoothly at each transition. I ran an 8-stage, 108-run comparison of time-series algorithms and IMU placements, using public MyPredict1 data to validate the selection and company data to train the deployed model. In a within-subject test on self-collected stair data, a 13-point ROCKET model reached 96.1% target recall with a 1.24% steady-state false-alarm rate, against a 90% bar. The algorithm shipped as a frozen ONNX + TensorRT FP16 model behind a ROS 2 topic interface on a Jetson Orin Nano; on-device, 57 real input windows produced no class change against the reference, at about 5 ms of inference and scheduling cost.

The model was only half of the work. Delsys IMUs output acceleration and angular rate but no reliable absolute attitude, so I built the input pipeline first: a 6-DoF ESKF (15-state error, no magnetometer, gravity alignment plus ZUPT on static segments) to rebuild sensor attitude, then an N-pose → one step → N-pose walking calibration for the world-to-human and sensor-to-bone rotations. The six IMUs' accelerometer magnitude and gyro bias were corrected offline, with parameters validated on data excluded from estimation, and their noise characterised with Allan variance. With that pipeline in place, the error could be split into three layers: device, heading and mounting. The paper's walking calibration and mine turned out to differ only in coordinate decomposition, leaving the final rotation almost unchanged; replacing the forearm sensor-to-bone rotation with a mocap-fitted version cut in-sample local rotation error from 19.63° to 16.29° across two trials, each fitted with its own trial's mocap. That shows the mounting rotation is one of the error sources; it is not a deployable calibration method. Encoder constraints and fine-tuning both degraded the global trajectory and were not adopted.

The same habit — measure the constraint, then decide — runs through the rest of my work. I added automatic mocap gait-event labelling to the existing annotation platform: rules generate IC/TC, start-stop and T1 terrain-transition candidates, turning a 10-minute trial that used to take about 90 minutes of manual labelling into 10–20 seconds of candidate generation plus human review; all newly collected training data now uses it. I proposed a force-plate-free insole calibration that combines static double-support constraints with CNN-BiLSTM dynamic force prediction, validated with a 15-subject leave-one-subject-out protocol on the Krumm dataset, reaching a normalized RMSE of 0.15 body weight for the dynamic reference in walking. I fine-tuned MedSAM's image encoder so it no longer depends on manual prompts, and cleaned a noisy training corpus so that a model as small as Qwen2.5-0.5B could actually learn from it.

I am finishing my MSc in Artificial Intelligence at CUHK, after a BEng in Electronic Information and Computer Engineering at CUHK-Shenzhen. Outside coursework I like problems with a hard number attached: a latency budget, an accuracy floor, a crash-recovery deadline.

experience.organization: Shenzhen Yunmostar Artificial Intelligence Co., Ltd.
experience.summary: Building the sensing algorithms that let a consumer exoskeleton read human intent, recognise locomotion transitions and estimate human pose in real time: from IMU scene-transition recognition to the input pipeline, device calibration and error attribution for sparse-IMU pose estimation.
highlights: Defined four assist states for a consumer exoskeleton — hold, up-transition, down-transition, back to level ground. Ran an 8-stage, 108-run comparison of time-series algorithms and IMU placements; on self-collected stair data, a 13-point ROCKET model reaches 96.1% target recall and a 1.24% steady-state false-alarm rate in a within-subject test (the bar was 90% on stairs).

Delivered a frozen ONNX + TensorRT FP16 model behind a ROS 2 (C++) topic interface and deployed it on a Jetson Orin Nano; on-device, 57 real input windows produced no class change against the reference, at about 5 ms of inference and scheduling cost.

Delsys IMUs expose only acceleration and angular rate, with no reliable absolute attitude. I configured a 6-DoF ESKF (15-state error, no magnetometer, gravity alignment and ZUPT on static segments) and implemented an N-pose → one step → N-pose walking calibration that recovers the world-to-human and sensor-to-bone rotations (RMB = RIMᵀ · RIS · RSB), so GlobalPose can consume company data directly. Without a magnetometer absolute heading stays unobservable, so heading analysis is done only after aligning the initial heading with mocap.

Calibrated six Delsys IMUs offline — accelerometer magnitude and gyroscope static bias — validated the parameters on independent data, and characterised ARW, VRW and bias instability with Allan variance. With gyro-bias-only correction the torso keeps leaning forward after large motions and the recovery segment stays at 12–13°; the full calibration brings the stair-and-high-knee sequence to 7–9°.

Reproduced GlobalPose and GRIP, two sparse-IMU human pose estimation methods, unified their evaluation protocol and selected GlobalPose; the old table's two headline errors came from different definitions, so they cannot justify the choice — I corrected that myself later in a protocol audit.

Localised the error source through matrix decomposition and single-variable substitution: the paper's walking calibration only changes the coordinate decomposition, with RIM and RIS each rotating by more than a hundred degrees and cancelling in the product. Replacing only the forearm sensor-to-bone rotation (RSB) with a mocap-fitted version cut in-sample local rotation error from 19.63° to 16.29° across 2 trials, each fitted with its own trial's mocap. Encoder constraints and fine-tuning both degraded the global trajectory and were not adopted.

Added automatic mocap gait-event labelling to the existing annotation platform: rule-generated IC/TC, start-stop and T1 terrain-transition candidates turn a 10-minute trial that used to take about 90 minutes of manual labelling into 10–20 seconds of candidate generation plus human review; all newly collected data now goes through it.

experience.role: Research — Predicting Ultrafast Nonlinear Dynamics in Fibre Optics with LSTM
experience.summary: Predicting ultrafast nonlinear dynamics in optical fibres is computationally expensive, and conventional numerical methods struggle with the complex-valued nature of the data.
highlights: Engineered a customized LSTM cell in Python designed to process complex-valued data, and trained the network on optical pulse propagation data under Prof. Yuan Luo.
Validated that recurrent neural networks can effectively forecast propagation pulses in optical fibres, demonstrating their capacity to handle complex data in nonlinear dynamic environments.

projects.title: Full-stack Live-stream E-commerce Auction System
projects.tagline: Millisecond bid synchronization without synchronous database writes.
highlights: Independent entry. Coding was AI-assisted; I designed the bidding path and the acceptance tests. The stack is React + TypeScript, Node.js + Socket.IO, Redis and MySQL, with one-click Docker deployment.

Bids run entirely as in-memory Redis operations with 5-second batch persistence to MySQL. The atomic Lua script became the default bidding path, replacing the original distributed-lock engine, alongside ZSet leaderboards, per-user rate limiting and a triple-heartbeat self-healing daemon.
The competition build reached 98.4% bid success with 11.4 ms average and 65 ms P99 round-trip at 1,000 concurrent WebSocket connections per live room (local benchmark).

Post-camp fixes raised same-millisecond burst success from 0.03% to 100% (199 ms average) across 3000 bids and cut downstream broadcast volume by about 430×; state is rebuilt from MySQL with leaderboard replay after Redis loss.

A post-event re-test found the server had accepted only 7 bids while the client reported 2934 successes. The load script was counting other bidders' success broadcasts; verifying each request ID made both sides agree.

projects.title: Prompt-free Breast Ultrasound Lesion Segmentation with MedSAM
projects.tagline: Removing MedSAM's dependence on manual position prompts.
highlights: MedSAM depends on manual position prompts and fails without them in an automated workflow; I benchmarked the unmodified model prompt-free to quantify that limit (IoU 0.093 on BUS-UCLM).
Froze the prompt encoder and fine-tuned the 90M-parameter ViT image encoder and mask decoder with a hybrid BCE and Dice loss, training on the BUS-UCLM training set only, with patient-level splits.
Improved IoU from 0.093 to 0.737 and F1 from 0.157 to 0.823 on BUS-UCLM (same-protocol U-Net: IoU 0.5414).
Generalized to an unseen, abnormal-only BUSI subset with IoU 0.591 vs. U-Net's 0.2603; BUSI was never used in training.
Reached 12 FPS at batch size 1 on a single RTX 4090.

projects.title: Data Cleaning and Full Fine-tuning for a Lightweight LLM
projects.tagline: Turning a noisy corpus into something a 0.5B model can actually learn from.
highlights: The raw OpenOrca subset had formatting issues, quality problems and semantic inconsistencies, which made it unsuitable for fine-tuning; I diagnosed them first, then designed a cleaning pipeline covering non-standard roles, missing fields, duplicate text and semantic consistency.
Kept 240,340 rows out of the first 1,000,000 for training.
Ran full supervised fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-0.5B in LLaMA-Factory on a single NVIDIA L4 (2 epochs).
Under an identical evaluation setup, MMLU (5-shot) improved from 0.253 to 0.400 and BoolQ from 0.632 to 0.718, while three PIQA and HellaSwag metrics decreased by 0.7–1.4 pt.

projects.title: Personalized Email Agent for a Campus Context
projects.tagline: On-device email triage that avoids cloud privacy risk and API cost.
highlights: Designed a multi-agent system on the ERNIE-Speed (10–15B) model using a parallel-serial pipeline.
Implemented Chain-of-Thought prompting and retrieval-augmented generation over a campus knowledge base.
Reached near-human labelling accuracy with precise extraction of course names, professors and deadlines, eliminating API costs and keeping deployment privacy-preserving and on-device.

Implemented gesture recognition for brick selection, rotation and placement using C# scripting.
Delivered a functional prototype that lets players build brick structures using hand gestures.

Designed the database schema for image storage, feature storage and picture matching.
Integrated Python feature extraction with MySQL storage and retrieval.

projects.title: 2-Player Bouncing Ball Game on a Cortex-M3 Board
projects.tagline: A real-time game on bare-metal embedded hardware.
highlights: Wrote C++ code to implement and synchronize GPIO, USART, LCD, external interrupts and timers on a Cortex-M3 development board.
Delivered a responsive two-player game on bare-metal hardware, with LCD, GPIO, USART, interrupts and timers all driven from C++.

projects.title: Two-pass MIPS Assembler
projects.tagline: Turning MIPS assembly into machine code while resolving forward labels.
highlights: Wrote a two-pass assembler in C++ with a shared label table: the first pass records label positions, the second encodes R-, I- and J-format instructions.
Resolved forward branch and jump targets before encoding, so a label can be referenced before its definition.
Compared the generated output with three course test programs and their expected machine code.
Documented the encoding rules, test cases and design in the project report.
